intro.text: This guide covers Module 1 of an 8-module plan that follows the GATE DA Probability & Statistics syllabus, not the much broader GATE Statistics (ST) paper.
Random variables — foundations (this guide): sample space, random variable, PMF, CDF, interval probabilities
Expectation and variance: mean, median, mode, E[g(X)], variance, standard deviation
Discrete distributions: discrete uniform, Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson
Continuous distributions: continuous uniform, exponential, normal, standard normal
t and chi-squared distributions: degrees of freedom, shapes, links to the normal
Multiple random variables: joint, marginal, conditional distributions; independence; covariance, correlation
Central Limit Theorem: sums and averages, normal approximation
Statistical inference: confidence intervals, z-, t- and chi-squared tests
Counting, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem come in as prerequisites wherever needed.

Syllabus trap: the DA syllabus lists Poisson among the continuous distributions. Poisson is discrete — it counts events (0, 1, 2, …). Answer exam questions by the mathematics, not by where the syllabus lists it.

sections.title: Lesson 1 — Random variables, PMF and CDF

blocks.text: 1. What is a random variable?
A random variable is a function that assigns a real number to each outcome of a random experiment. It is not the experiment itself, and despite the name it is not a "variable" in the algebra sense.
Example. Toss two fair coins. The sample space is:
S = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\}
Define X = number of heads. X maps each outcome to a number:
Illustration description: Random variable: each of the four outcomes is mapped to a number of heads

Four outcomes collapse to three values, so X ∈ {0, 1, 2}. The set of values X can take is called its support. Two different outcomes (HT and TH) map to the same value — that is allowed, because a function can be many-to-one.

Discrete vs continuous. X is discrete when its support is finite or countable (heads, defects, arrivals). It is continuous when it can take any value in an interval (time, height, voltage). Discrete variables get a PMF; continuous ones get a PDF. Both have a CDF.
2. Probability Mass Function (PMF)

The PMF gives the probability that a discrete X takes each exact value: p(x) = P(X = x). For two fair, independent tosses each outcome has probability 1/4, so X = 1 (HT or TH) gets 1/2 — twice as likely as 0 or 2 heads.
Illustration description: PMF of the number of heads: 1/4, 1/2, 1/4
p_X(x) = \begin{cases} \tfrac14 & x = 0 \\ \tfrac12 & x = 1 \\ \tfrac14 & x = 2 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
A function is a valid PMF only if both hold:
p(x) ≥ 0 for every x
The probabilities over the support add to 1:
\sum_x p_X(x) = 1 \qquad \text{here: } \tfrac14 + \tfrac12 + \tfrac14 = 1
The probability of any set A of values is the sum of p(x) over the values in A. Example: P(X is odd) = P(X = 1) = 1/2.
3. Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF)
The CDF accumulates probability up to and including x:
F_X(x) = P(X \le x)
Illustration description: CDF of the number of heads as a step function: 0, 0.25, 0.75, 1

Read the graph carefully. For a discrete X the CDF is a staircase. It is defined for every real x, not only 0, 1, 2 — e.g. F(1.7) = 0.75 and F(−3) = 0. At each jump the filled dot is on the upper step (the value includes the jump); the open dot marks the value just before it. Each jump height equals p(x) at that point.
Properties every CDF satisfies (GATE tests these):
Non-decreasing: if a < b then F(a) ≤ F(b)
F(x) → 0 as x → −∞ and F(x) → 1 as x → +∞
Right-continuous (that is why the filled dot sits on the upper step)
Interval probabilities from the CDF — mind the endpoints for discrete X:

blocks.tex: P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a) \qquad P(X = a) = F(a) - F(a^-) \qquad P(X > a) = 1 - F(a)
blocks.text: P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a) \qquad P(X = a) = F(a) - F(a^-) \qquad P(X > a) = 1 - F(a)
PMF vs CDF in one line: the PMF is the probability at a value; the CDF is the probability up to and including a value.
4. GATE-style numerical: find the missing constant
Question. P(X = x) = c(x + 1) for x = 0, 1, 2 and 0 otherwise. Find c, then P(X ≥ 1).
Illustration description: Worked solution: c + 2c + 3c = 1 gives c = 1/6, and P(X ≥ 1) = 5/6
Normalise. Total probability must be 1:
c(0+1) + c(1+1) + c(2+1) = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; 6c = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; c = \tfrac16
Write out the PMF. P(X=0) = 1/6, P(X=1) = 2/6, P(X=2) = 3/6.
Check non-negativity. All three are ≥ 0, so c = 1/6 gives a valid PMF. (In harder questions — e.g. P(X=x) = c(x − 1) — this check is what rules out a candidate value of c.)
Answer the event. Use the complement, which is faster when the event covers most of the support:
P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - \tfrac16 = \tfrac56
Method to memorise: normalise → list the PMF → check p(x) ≥ 0 → sum (or use the complement) for the event.
5. Practice questions
Try all five before reading the answers below.
☐ Q1. A fair coin is tossed three times; X = number of heads. P(X = 2) = ? (A) 1/8 (B) 2/8 (C) 3/8 (D) 1/2
☐ Q2. P(X = x) = kx² for x = 1, 2, 3 (0 otherwise). Find k and P(X ≤ 2).
☐ Q3. A discrete X has CDF F(x) = 0 for x < 1; 0.3 for 1 ≤ x < 3; 0.7 for 3 ≤ x < 5; 1 for x ≥ 5. Find P(X = 3), P(X < 3) and P(1 < X ≤ 5).
☐ Q4. For the two-coin X of this guide, find F(1.5) and F(−0.2).
☐ Q5. Two fair dice are rolled; X = the larger of the two numbers. Find P(X = 3).
Answers
(C) 3/8. Outcomes with two heads: HHT, HTH, THH = 3 of 8.
F(1.5) = 0.75, F(−0.2) = 0. The CDF is flat between support points.
5/36. P(X ≤ 3) = (3/6)² = 9/36 and P(X ≤ 2) = 4/36, so P(X = 3) = 9/36 − 4/36. This is the CDF-difference trick: it is often easier to find F first and take the jump.
6. Revision sheet

rows: Function from outcomes to real numbers
Many outcomes can map to one value
Set of values X can take

blocks.text: Common mistakes
Treating HT and TH as one outcome — they are separate, each with probability 1/4.
Mixing ≤ and < for discrete X: P(X < 3) ≠ P(X ≤ 3) when P(X = 3) > 0.
Evaluating the CDF only at support points; it is defined (and flat) everywhere in between.
Forgetting to check p(x) ≥ 0 after solving for a constant.
Calling Poisson continuous because of the syllabus wording.
Next: Module 2 — expectation and variance, built on the same two-coin PMF.

sections.title: Lesson 2 — Discrete vs Continuous Random Variables

blocks.text: Infinitely many possible values does not make a random variable continuous. What matters is whether the values can be listed in a sequence (discrete) or fill a whole interval (continuous).
7. Discrete does not mean finite
A random variable is discrete when its possible values can be listed as a sequence — finite or countably infinite.
Example. Toss a fair coin until the first head. X = number of tosses needed.
Illustration description: Tosses until the first head: P(X = k) = (1/2)^k, values 1, 2, 3, 4, … go on forever
X ∈ {1, 2, 3, …} has infinitely many values, but X can never be 2.5 or 3.78 — there are gaps between allowed values. So X is discrete. The first head on toss k needs k − 1 tails then a head:
P(X = k) = \left(\tfrac12\right)^{k-1} \cdot \tfrac12 = \left(\tfrac12\right)^{k}, \qquad k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots
Is it a valid PMF? Every term is positive, and the infinite geometric series sums to 1:
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left(\tfrac12\right)^k = \frac{1/2}{1 - 1/2} = 1
This is the geometric distribution (with p = 1/2). In general, for success probability p: P(X = k) = (1 − p)^(k−1) · p. It is a standard source of GATE questions on infinite sums.
8. Continuous random variables
A random variable is continuous when it can take every real value in an interval, with no gaps between allowed values.
Example. Y = waiting time for a bus, anywhere from 0 to 10 minutes, so Y ∈ [0, 10]. Between 2 and 3 alone, Y could be 2.5, 2.57, 2.5789, … — however far you zoom in, there are more possible values.
Illustration description: Bus waiting time: any real value between 0 and 10 minutes is possible
This set of values is uncountable: unlike {1, 2, 3, …}, it cannot be listed as a sequence. That — not "infinitely many" — is what separates continuous from discrete.

Count vs measure. Counting things (customers, defects, tosses) gives discrete variables. Measuring things (time, length, weight) usually gives continuous ones. The word "usually" matters: an amount of money recorded to the paisa is discrete in strict terms, although it is often modelled as continuous.
Illustration description: Number of customers (counted) is discrete and uses a PMF; time between arrivals (measured) is continuous and uses a PDF

Correction to this image: the right-hand bell-shaped curve is only a sketch. In the standard model, time between random arrivals follows an exponential distribution, whose PDF is highest at 0 and falls steadily — not a hump. You will meet it in Module 4.
9. The key GATE difference: points vs intervals
For a continuous variable, the probability of any single exact value is zero; only intervals carry probability, and that probability is the area under the density curve.
Illustration description: For continuous Y, P(Y = 3) = 0 (a line has no area) but P(3 ≤ Y ≤ 5) > 0 (shaded area)
Three consequences GATE tests:
Endpoints don't matter for continuous Y. P(3 ≤ Y ≤ 5) = P(3 < Y < 5) = P(3 ≤ Y < 5). For discrete X they can differ (see Lesson 1, Q3).
Zero probability ≠ impossible. Waiting exactly 3.000… minutes can happen; it just carries no probability on its own.
A PDF value is not a probability. f(y) is a density and can be greater than 1 (e.g. a uniform PDF on [0, 0.5] equals 2). Only areas are probabilities, so total area must be 1.
We will derive the PDF and these area calculations properly in the next lesson.
10. Lesson 2 practice

☐ Q1. A shop has X = number of customers arriving and Y = time between two arrivals. Which is correct? (A) Both discrete, since customers arrive one at a time (B) X discrete, Y continuous (C) Both continuous, since the number of customers can be arbitrarily large (D) X continuous, Y discrete
☐ Q2. Discrete or continuous? (a) emails received in a day (b) a student's height (c) rolls of a die until the first six (d) proportion of defective items in a batch of 100
☐ Q3. For X = tosses until the first head (fair coin), find P(X > 3) and P(X is even).
☐ Q4. P(X = k) = c(1/3)^k for k = 0, 1, 2, … Find c.
☐ Q5. Y is continuous and P(Y ≤ 4) = 0.6. Find P(Y < 4) and P(Y = 4).
☐ Q6. True or false: a PDF with f(2) = 1.5 cannot be valid.
Answers
(B). X is a count with values 0, 1, 2, …; Y is a measured time that can be any non-negative real. (C) is the exact trap of this lesson: unbounded does not mean continuous.
(a) discrete (b) continuous (c) discrete — infinitely many values but countable (d) discrete — only 0, 0.01, 0.02, …, 1 are possible, even though it is a fraction.
P(X > 3) = 1/8: the first three tosses must all be tails, (1/2)³. P(X even) = 1/3: (1/4) + (1/16) + … = (1/4)/(1 − 1/4).
c = 2/3. c · 1/(1 − 1/3) = 1 → c · 3/2 = 1. Note the sum starts at k = 0 here.
P(Y < 4) = 0.6, P(Y = 4) = 0. The endpoint carries no probability.
False. A density can exceed 1; only the total area must equal 1.
11. Lesson 2 revision sheet
Discrete = values can be listed in a sequence (finite or countably infinite). Uses a PMF; probabilities are sums.
Continuous = values fill an interval (uncountable). Uses a PDF; probabilities are areas.
Test to apply: "Is there a gap between one allowed value and the next?" Yes → discrete. No → continuous.
Geometric (first success): P(X = k) = (1 − p)^(k−1) · p, k = 1, 2, …; and P(X > n) = (1 − p)^n.
Common mistakes
Calling a variable continuous because it is unbounded or has infinitely many values.
Calling a proportion or average continuous when it comes from a finite count.
Adding a point probability like P(Y = 3) for continuous Y — it is always 0.
Treating f(y) as a probability, or rejecting a PDF because some f(y) > 1.
Worrying about ≤ vs < for continuous Y (it doesn't matter) but ignoring it for discrete X (it does).
Next: Lesson 3 — PMF vs PDF in depth: why point probability is zero, computing areas, and the CDF of a continuous variable.
A PDF does not give probabilities directly: it gives a density, and the probability of an interval is the area under the PDF over that interval.
12. Why we need a PDF: density = probability per unit

For discrete X we can write P(X = 1) = 1/2 directly. For continuous Y every single value has probability 0 (Lesson 2), so a PMF would be zero everywhere. We need a function that tells us how probability is spread along the line — the probability density function f(y).

Example. Y = bus waiting time, uniformly distributed on [0, 10] minutes: equal-length intervals are equally likely, so waiting 1–2 minutes is as likely as waiting 7–8 minutes. The total probability 1 is spread evenly over 10 minutes:
f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{10} = 0.1 & 0 \le y \le 10 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
Illustration description: Uniform(0, 10): density 0.1 per minute; 3–5 minutes gives 0.20, 3–3.5 minutes gives 0.05
The height 0.1 is a rate: 0.1 probability per minute. Multiply by a width to get a probability:
3 to 5 minutes: 2 × 0.1 = 0.20
Same density, different widths, different probabilities. In general, for a small width Δy:

blocks.tex: P(y \le Y \le y + \Delta y) \approx f_Y(y)\,\Delta y
blocks.text: P(y \le Y \le y + \Delta y) \approx f_Y(y)\,\Delta y
This is why density has units (per minute, per kg…), while probability has none.
13. Probability is area: interval vs single point
The PDF's height at a point is not the probability of that point. For the uniform bus model, f(3) = 0.1 but P(Y = 3) = 0.
Illustration description: f(3) = 0.1 but P(Y = 3) = 0; P(3 ≤ Y ≤ 5) = 2 × 0.1 = 0.2
Why the point probability is 0. Fix the start at 3 and shrink the end towards 3:
As the width goes to 0, the area goes to 0. In integral form, an integral over a single point is always zero:
Image note: the left panel labels the point "x = 3" although the variable is Y; read it as y = 3.
14. PDF rules, PMF vs PDF, and the CDF link
A function f is a valid PDF if and only if both hold:
Non-negative: f(x) ≥ 0 for all x
Total area 1:
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1 \qquad \text{bus example: } \int_0^{10} 0.1\,dy = 0.1 \times 10 = 1
There is no rule that f(x) ≤ 1. Uniform on [0, 0.5] has f = 2 everywhere on its range and is perfectly valid (area 0.5 × 2 = 1).
Illustration description: PMF assigns probability to a single value; a PDF is a density whose area gives probability
The CDF link (used constantly in GATE). The CDF of a continuous variable is the accumulated area, and the PDF is its derivative:

blocks.tex: F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t)\,dt, \qquad f(x) = \frac{dF(x)}{dx}, \qquad P(a \le X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)
blocks.text: F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t)\,dt, \qquad f(x) = \frac{dF(x)}{dx}, \qquad P(a \le X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)

Bus example: F(y) = 0 for y < 0, y/10 for 0 ≤ y ≤ 10, and 1 for y > 10. Check: F(5) − F(3) = 0.5 − 0.3 = 0.2 ✔. Unlike the discrete staircase of Lesson 1, this CDF is a continuous ramp with no jumps — which is exactly why no single point has positive probability.
15. GATE numericals on PDFs
Example A — rectangular PDF
f(x) = 0.2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 5, and 0 otherwise. Find P(1 ≤ X ≤ 4). Options: (A) 0.2 (B) 0.4 (C) 0.6 (D) 0.8.
Illustration description: Check validity (area 5 × 0.2 = 1), then P(1 ≤ X ≤ 4) = 3 × 0.2 = 0.6
Valid? f ≥ 0 and area = 5 × 0.2 = 1 ✔
Area over [1, 4]: width 3 × height 0.2 = 0.6 → (C)
Example B — non-rectangular PDF with unknown k
When the PDF is not flat, "width × height" fails; you must integrate. f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, and 0 otherwise. Find k, P(X ≤ 1) and P(X = 1).
Normalise:
\int_0^2 kx\,dx = k\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^2 = 2k = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; k = \tfrac12
Check non-negativity: x/2 ≥ 0 on [0, 2] ✔
Integrate over the event:
P(X \le 1) = \int_0^1 \frac{x}{2}\,dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{4}\right]_0^1 = \tfrac14
Point probability: P(X = 1) = 0, even though f(1) = 0.5.
Trap: [0, 1] is half the support, but the probability is only 1/4, not 1/2 — the density is low near 0 and high near 2. Half the width gives half the probability only for a uniform PDF.
Method to memorise: normalise (∫ f = 1) → check f ≥ 0 → integrate f over the event (or use F(b) − F(a)) → ignore endpoints.
16. Lesson 3 practice
☐ Q1. Y ~ Uniform(0, 10). Find P(Y > 7) and P(2 < Y ≤ 2.5).
☐ Q2. f(x) = k for 2 ≤ x ≤ 6, 0 otherwise. Find k and P(X < 3).
☐ Q3. f(x) = 3 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1/3, 0 otherwise. Is it a valid PDF? Find P(X = 0.1) and P(X ≤ 0.1).
☐ Q4. f(x) = c(1 − x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 otherwise. Find c and P(X > 1/2).
☐ Q5. f(x) = kx² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3, 0 otherwise. Find k and P(1 ≤ X ≤ 2).
☐ Q6. A continuous X has CDF F(x) = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 (0 below, 1 above). Find its PDF and P(0.5 < X ≤ 1).
☐ Q7. Which is a valid PDF? (A) f(x) = 2x on [0, 1] (B) f(x) = x − 1 on [0, 2] (C) f(x) = 1/2 on [0, 3]
Answers
0.3 and 0.05. Widths 3 and 0.5, each × 0.1.
k = 1/4, P(X < 3) = 1/4. Width 4 × k = 1; then width 1 × 1/4.
Valid (3 ≥ 0, area (1/3) × 3 = 1 — a density above 1 is fine). P(X = 0.1) = 0, P(X ≤ 0.1) = 0.1 × 3 = 0.3.
c = 2, P(X > 1/2) = 1/4. ∫₀¹ c(1 − x) dx = c/2 = 1. Then ∫ from 1/2 to 1 of 2(1 − x) dx = 2 × 1/8. (A triangle: the right half holds only a quarter of the area.)
f(x) = 2x on [0, 1]; P = 0.75. Differentiate F; then F(1) − F(0.5) = 1 − 0.25.
(A). (B) is negative on [0, 1); (C) has total area 1.5, not 1.
17. Lesson 3 revision sheet
Common mistakes
Reading f(a) as P(X = a).
Rejecting a PDF because some value is above 1.
Using width × height when the PDF is not flat — integrate instead.
Assuming half the range means half the probability for a non-uniform PDF.
Forgetting to check f ≥ 0 after finding k.
Next: Lesson 4 — Solving PDFs using integration.
When a PDF's height changes along the range, probability is still area, but the area must be found by integration: P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx.
18. Changing density: why we integrate
With a flat PDF, probability = width × height. With f(x) = 2x on [0, 1], the height changes with x, so there is no single height to multiply by.
The density rises to the right, so equal-width intervals near 1 hold more probability than those near 0.
Illustration description: Constant height: rectangle area 2 × 0.1 = 0.2. Changing height: add thin strips, i.e. integrate
Integration slices the region into very thin strips of width dx and height f(x), and adds their areas f(x)·dx:
P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx
The one rule you need for most GATE PDFs is the power rule:

blocks.tex: \int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \quad (n \ne -1), \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = G(b) - G(a) \text{ where } G' = f
blocks.text: \int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \quad (n \ne -1), \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = G(b) - G(a) \text{ where } G' = f
19. Worked numerical: f(x) = 2x
Question. f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, 0 otherwise. Is it a valid PDF? Find P(0 ≤ X ≤ 0.5).
Illustration description: f(x) = 2x: P(0 ≤ X ≤ 0.5) = 0.25 by integration and by triangle area; total area = 1
Validity. 2x ≥ 0 on [0, 1], and
\int_0^1 2x\,dx = \left[x^2\right]_0^1 = 1 - 0 = 1 \;\checkmark
Integrate over the event. The antiderivative of 2x is x²; evaluate at the upper limit minus the lower limit:
Geometric check. The shaded region is a triangle with base 0.5 and height f(0.5) = 1: area = ½ × 0.5 × 1 = 0.25 ✔. (The image's "Height =" label is missing its value — it is 1.)
Observation. Half the range [0, 0.5] holds only 25% of the probability; the other half holds 75%. In general here P(X ≤ a) = a², so F(x) = x² on [0, 1] — the same CDF you met in Lesson 3, Q6.
f(1) = 2 is fine: density can exceed 1, only total area must be 1.
20. Support: where the distribution lives
The support is the set of values X can actually take: a list of points for a discrete X, an interval (or union of intervals) where f > 0 for a continuous X.
Illustration description: Discrete support {0, 1, 2} vs continuous support [0, 1] for f(x) = 2x
Why it matters in numericals: outside the support f = 0, so integrals only run over the part of the event that overlaps the support. Clip the limits first.
Example with f(x) = x/2 on [0, 2]:
P(X ≤ 3) = ∫₀² (x/2) dx = 1 — the upper limit 3 is clipped to 2.
P(−1 ≤ X ≤ 1) = ∫₀¹ (x/2) dx = 1/4 — the lower limit −1 is clipped to 0.
For a piecewise PDF, split the integral at each break point and use the right formula on each piece (see Q7 below).

On the image's footnote: f(0) = 0 does not exclude 0 from the support — it is the boundary of [0, 1]. For a continuous X this makes no difference to any probability, since single points carry zero probability.
21. GATE numerical: find k, then the probability
Question. f(x) = kx for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, 0 otherwise. Find k and P(1 ≤ X ≤ 2). (Same PDF as Lesson 3, Example B — here we ask for the other half.)
Illustration description: Find k = 1/2 from total area 1; draw f(x) = x/2; P(1 ≤ X ≤ 2) = 3/4
Total area = 1:
\int_0^2 kx\,dx = k\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^2 = 2k = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; k = \tfrac12, \qquad f(x) = \tfrac{x}{2}
Integrate over [1, 2]:
P(1 \le X \le 2) = \int_1^2 \frac{x}{2}\,dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{4}\right]_1^2 = 1 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac34
Cross-check: Lesson 3 found P(0 ≤ X ≤ 1) = 1/4, and 1/4 + 3/4 = 1 ✔. A second check: the green region is a trapezium with parallel sides 0.5 and 1 and width 1, area ½(0.5 + 1)(1) = 0.75 ✔.
Exam shortcut: when the question asks for most of the range, compute the small complement and subtract from 1.
22. Lesson 4 practice
☐ Q3. f(x) = kx³ for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Find k and P(X ≤ 1).
☐ Q4. f(x) = k(2 − x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Find k and P(X ≤ 1).
☐ Q5. f(x) = x/2 on [0, 2]. Find P(X ≤ 3) and P(X > 2.5).
☐ Q6. Is f(x) = 6x(1 − x) on [0, 1] a valid PDF? If so, find P(X ≤ 1/2).
☐ Q7. Piecewise PDF: f(x) = x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1, f(x) = 2 − x for 1 < x ≤ 2, 0 otherwise. Find P(0.5 ≤ X ≤ 1.5).
Answers
(A) 0.125. ∫₀^0.5 3x² dx = [x³]₀^0.5 = 0.125. Trap: 0.375 is width × height at the right end (0.5 × f(0.5)), which overcounts because the curve is lower to the left.
k = 1/2, P(X ≤ 1) = 3/4. ∫₀² k(2 − x) dx = k(4 − 2) = 2k. Then ½[2x − x²/2]₀¹ = ½(1.5). Mirror image of f = x/2, so the answer flips from 1/4 to 3/4.
1 and 0. Both events are clipped by the support [0, 2].
Valid, P = 1/2. f ≥ 0 on [0, 1]; ∫ (6x − 6x²) dx = [3x² − 2x³]₀¹ = 1. At 1/2: 3/4 − 1/4 = 1/2 (the PDF is symmetric about 1/2).

0.75. Split at 1: ∫ from 0.5 to 1 of x dx = 0.375, plus ∫ from 1 to 1.5 of (2 − x) dx = 0.375. Geometric check: the whole triangle has area 1, and the two cut-off corner triangles each have area ½ × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125, so 1 − 0.25.
23. Lesson 4 revision sheet
Find k: set ∫ over the support of f(x) dx = 1, solve for k.
Check f ≥ 0 on the whole support with that k.
Clip the event to the support, split at any piecewise break points.
Integrate: antiderivative at upper limit minus at lower limit.
Check: triangle or trapezium area for straight-line PDFs, or confirm complements add to 1.
Common mistakes
Using width × height on a sloping PDF.
Forgetting to divide by n + 1 in the power rule (∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4, not x⁴).
Integrating past the support instead of clipping the limits.
Using one formula across a piecewise PDF instead of splitting.
Swapping the limits (lower − upper) and getting a negative "probability".
Next: Lesson 5 — The CDF of a continuous random variable.

sections.title: Lesson 5 — The CDF of a Continuous Random Variable

blocks.text: The CDF F(x) = P(X ≤ x) records the area under the PDF from the far left up to x. Integrate f to get F; differentiate F to get f.
24. What the CDF is: accumulated probability
If you answer P(X ≤ 0.3), P(X ≤ 0.6) and P(X ≤ 0.9) one integral at a time, you repeat the same work. The CDF does it once, for every x:
F(x) = P(X \le x)
Capital F is the CDF; small f is the PDF. Picture walking left to right under f(x) = 2x and recording the area behind you: 0 at x = 0, 0.36 at x = 0.6, all of it (1) at x = 1.
Illustration description: F(0.6) = area under f(x) = 2x from 0 to 0.6 = 0.36, i.e. 36% accumulated
Note f(0.6) = 1.2 is the height of the PDF, not a probability; F(0.6) = 0.36 is the probability.
25. From PDF to CDF: integrate
F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{x} f(t)\,dt
The dummy variable t keeps the moving integration variable separate from the upper limit x.
Example. f(x) = 2x on [0, 1].
Support is [0, 1]; there is no density below 0, so start the integral at 0.
Integrate for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1:
F(x) = \int_0^x 2t\,dt = \left[t^2\right]_0^x = x^2
Fill in every region — the CDF is defined for all real x, and GATE marks you down for leaving regions out:
F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \\ x^2 & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 1 & x > 1 \end{cases}
Illustration description: Integrate f(x) = 2x to get F(x) = x² on [0, 1], 0 to the left and 1 to the right

Shape check: a straight rising PDF gives a curved CDF; the CDF is steepest where the PDF is tallest (near x = 1), because its slope is the PDF. The pieces join with no jumps: F = 0 at x = 0 and F = 1 at x = 1 from both sides.
26. Using the CDF: intervals and tails
Once F is known, no more integration is needed — just plug in and subtract.
For a continuous X, < and ≤ give the same answer, since P(X = a) = 0. So P(0.5 < X < 0.8) is also 0.39. (For a discrete X this is not true — recall Lesson 1, Q3.)
Values outside the support: P(X ≤ 1.7) = F(1.7) = 1 and P(X > −2) = 1 − F(−2) = 1. Read off the correct region of the piecewise CDF; don't plug 1.7 into x².
27. From CDF back to PDF, and CDF properties
Differentiate the CDF to recover the PDF (wherever F is differentiable):

blocks.tex: f(x) = \frac{dF(x)}{dx} \qquad \text{e.g. } \frac{d}{dx}(x^2) = 2x \text{ on } 0 < x < 1, \text{ and } f = 0 \text{ elsewhere}
blocks.text: f(x) = \frac{dF(x)}{dx} \qquad \text{e.g. } \frac{d}{dx}(x^2) = 2x \text{ on } 0 < x < 1, \text{ and } f = 0 \text{ elsewhere}
Illustration description: PDF and CDF linked by integration and differentiation; the CDF properties
Every CDF satisfies:
Non-decreasing
F(x) → 0 as x → −∞, and F(x) → 1 as x → +∞
Right-continuous

For a continuous random variable the CDF is more than right-continuous: it is continuous everywhere, with no jumps. Image note: the open dot drawn at the origin of the CDF graph suggests a jump at x = 0. There is none — F(0) = 0 from both sides. Open and filled dots belong to discrete (staircase) CDFs, as in Lesson 1.
Checking a proposed CDF (common GATE MCQ): test each property. F(x) = 1 − x on [0, 1] fails (decreasing). F(x) = 2x on [0, 1] fails (exceeds 1). F(x) = x² on [0, 1] with 0 below and 1 above passes.
28. Harder GATE patterns
A. Median and percentiles: solve F(m) = target
The median m is the value with half the probability on each side: F(m) = 0.5. The p-th percentile solves F(x) = p/100.
For F(x) = x² on [0, 1]:
m^2 = 0.5 \;\Rightarrow\; m = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.707 \qquad \text{75th percentile: } x^2 = 0.75 \Rightarrow x \approx 0.866
The median is above 0.5 because the density is piled up on the right.
B. CDF of a piecewise PDF: carry the accumulated area forward
Triangle PDF: f(x) = x on [0, 1], f(x) = 2 − x on [1, 2], 0 otherwise.
0 ≤ x ≤ 1: F(x) = ∫₀ˣ t dt = x²/2. At x = 1, F = 1/2.
1 ≤ x ≤ 2: start from the 1/2 already accumulated, then add the new piece:
F(x) = \tfrac12 + \int_1^x (2 - t)\,dt = \tfrac12 + \left[2t - \tfrac{t^2}{2}\right]_1^x = 2x - \tfrac{x^2}{2} - 1

blocks.tex: F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \\ x^2/2 & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 2x - x^2/2 - 1 & 1 < x \le 2 \\ 1 & x > 2 \end{cases}
blocks.text: F(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \\ x^2/2 & 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 2x - x^2/2 - 1 & 1 < x \le 2 \\ 1 & x > 2 \end{cases}
The classic mistake is starting the second piece from 0 instead of from F(1) = 1/2. Check the join values every time.
29. Lesson 5 practice
☐ Q1. A continuous X has CDF F(x) = x² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. P(X > 0.6) = ? (A) 0.36 (B) 0.40 (C) 0.64 (D) 0.60
☐ Q2. f(x) = x/2 on [0, 2]. Write the full CDF, then find P(X ≤ 1.5) and P(X > 1).
☐ Q3. F(x) = x³ on [0, 1] (0 below, 1 above). Find the PDF and P(0.5 < X ≤ 1).
☐ Q4. For f(x) = 2x on [0, 1], find the median and the 75th percentile.
☐ Q5. Which can be a CDF on [0, 1] (0 below, 1 above)? (A) x² (B) 1 − x (C) 2x
☐ Q6. F(x) = 1 − e^(−2x) for x ≥ 0, 0 for x < 0. Find the PDF and P(X > 1).
☐ Q7. A continuous X has F(x) = kx² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3, 0 below, 1 above. Find k, the PDF, and P(1 < X < 2).
☐ Q8. For the triangle PDF of section 28B, find P(X ≤ 1.5) and the median.
Answers
(C) 0.64. 1 − F(0.6) = 1 − 0.36. Option (A) is F(0.6) itself — the left tail, not the right.
Median ≈ 0.707, 75th percentile ≈ 0.866. Solve x² = 0.5 and x² = 0.75.
(A). (B) decreases; (C) exceeds 1 for x > 0.5.
f(x) = 2e^(−2x) for x ≥ 0; P(X > 1) = e^(−2) ≈ 0.135. This is the exponential distribution — you'll meet it in Module 4.
k = 1/9, f(x) = 2x/9 on [0, 3], P = 1/3. Continuity at 3 forces k·9 = 1. Then (4 − 1)/9.
P(X ≤ 1.5) = 0.875; median = 1. Second piece: 3 − 1.125 − 1 = 0.875. F(1) = 1/2, so the median is 1 (the PDF is symmetric about 1).

blocks.text: Common mistakes
Answering a right-tail question with F(a) instead of 1 − F(a).
Plugging a value outside the support into the middle formula (F(1.7) = 1, not 1.7²).
Writing only the middle piece of the CDF.
Restarting a piecewise CDF from 0 at the break point.
Confusing f(a) (height) with F(a) (probability).
